questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of counting sort?

answer.text: Count how many times each key occurs, take prefix sums to find positions, then place each element into its output slot

feedback.text: Correct — count, prefix-sum, then place.

answer.text: Repeatedly select the minimum remaining element and append it

feedback.text: That is selection sort, a comparison sort.

answer.text: Divide the array in half, sort each half, and merge

feedback.text: That is merge sort.

answer.text: Choose a pivot and partition the array around it recursively

feedback.text: That is quicksort.

generalfeedback.text: Counting sort tallies key frequencies, converts the counts into starting positions via prefix sums, then scatters elements into a stable output array.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of counting sort, where k is the range of key values?

feedback.text: Correct — linear in the number of elements plus the size of the key range.
That is the comparison-sort bound; counting sort is not comparison-based.
Counting sort never needs quadratic time.
There is no log factor; both the count and placement passes are linear.

generalfeedback.text: One pass counts (O(n)), one pass builds prefix sums over the range (O(k)), one pass places elements (O(n)) — total O(n + k).

questiontext.text: Counting sort is efficient (effectively linear) only when which condition holds?

answer.text: The key range k is O(n), i.e. a small integer range relative to the element count

feedback.text: Correct — when k = O(n), O(n + k) collapses to O(n).

answer.text: The keys are arbitrary floating-point numbers

feedback.text: Counting sort indexes by integer key and cannot directly bucket arbitrary floats.

answer.text: The array is already nearly sorted

feedback.text: Counting sort's cost does not depend on initial order.

answer.text: The range k is much larger than n

feedback.text: A huge range makes O(n + k) dominated by k and wastes space.

generalfeedback.text: Counting sort shines when the key range is small (k = O(n)); a range far larger than n makes it slow and memory-hungry.

questiontext.text: Counting sort is stable when elements are placed by iterating the input from right to left using the prefix-sum positions.

feedback.text: Correct — right-to-left placement preserves the original order of equal keys.
Counting sort is a classic stable sort.

questiontext.text: Counting sort is a comparison-based algorithm bound by the Ω(n log n) lower bound.

feedback.text: No — it indexes by key value and never compares two elements, so it can be linear.
Correct — counting sort is not comparison-based.

questiontext.text: To turn the per-key counts into starting output positions, counting sort computes the ______ sums of the count array (English term, e.g. "prefix").

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct — cumulative sums serve the same purpose.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Counting sort becomes impractical when the key ______ (the spread of possible key values) is very large. Fill in the English word.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about counting sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Its auxiliary space is O(n + k)

feedback.text: Yes — a count array of size k plus an output array of size n.

answer.text: It is well suited to sorting small non-negative integers

feedback.text: Yes — that is exactly its sweet spot.

answer.text: It can sort arbitrary floating-point keys directly without transformation

feedback.text: No — it indexes by integer keys and cannot bucket raw floats directly.

answer.text: It works by comparing pairs of elements

feedback.text: No — it never compares elements; it counts keys.

generalfeedback.text: Counting sort needs O(n + k) space, excels on small integer keys, cannot directly handle raw floats, and performs no comparisons.
